subtopics.title: Origin of International Labour Day
subtopics.summary: International Labour Day, also called Workers Day or May Day, is observed every year on May 1 to honour the contribution of workers. Its origin is traced to the late 19th century labour movement in the United States, where workers demanded an eight-hour working day. A large 1886 demonstration in Chicago went out of hand, and the incident known as the Haymarket Affair marked the start of the day. In 1889, Socialist Parties in Europe decided to celebrate May 1 as International Labour Day.

subtopics.title: Constitutional provisions and labour laws
subtopics.summary: The Constitution gives citizens the right to form associations or unions and prohibits forced labour and employment of children below 14 years. Articles 39(a), 41, 43 and 43A set out goals for the State on livelihood, work, a living wage and worker participation in management. Labour legislation includes laws on factories, wages, provident funds and industrial disputes. Four labour codes together amalgamate 29 laws.

subtopics.title: International Labour Organisation: profile
subtopics.summary: The International Labour Organisation is a specialised agency of the United Nations dedicated to improving labour conditions and living standards throughout the world. It was established under the Treaty of Versailles and became the first specialised agency associated with the UN in 1946. Its tripartite structure gives an equal voice to governments, employers and workers. The ILO was awarded the Nobel Prize for Peace in 1969, and its headquarters is in Geneva, Switzerland.

subtopics.title: ILO objectives, standards and reports
subtopics.summary: The ILO pursues four stated objectives: promoting fundamental labour rights, creating greater opportunities for women and men, enhancing social protection, and strengthening social dialogue and tripartism. Its international labour standards are Conventions and Protocols, which are legally binding treaties, and Recommendations, which are non-binding guidelines. The ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work, adopted in 1998, names focus areas such as freedom of association and abolition of child labour. The ILO also publishes key reports, including the Global Wage Report.

quizzes.title: Constitution and labour laws: practice set
quizzes.passage: Labour welfare in India is shaped by two sources of authority: the Constitution and a body of ordinary statutes. The Constitution does not only grant rights to individuals; it also sets out aims that the State is expected to pursue. Some provisions protect workers from being made to work against their will, while others shield young people from early employment. Other provisions describe the kind of economic life the State should aim for, including a means of livelihood, employment within economic capacity, fair pay and a voice for workers in the industries where they work. Parliament has translated many of these aims into laws covering factories, wages, provident funds, compensation and disputes between employers and employees. Several of these statutes have since been grouped into a smaller number of broad codes. The codes group rules on wages, industrial relations, social security and occupational safety and health. Each statute addresses a specific aspect of work, such as the payment of wages, the settlement of disputes or compensation to workers. Labour matters also have an international dimension, since a United Nations agency works to improve labour conditions and living standards across the world. Together, these provisions and laws show that labour protection in India has both a constitutional foundation and a statutory one.

questions.q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution prohibits employment of children below the age of 14 years?

questions.q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution orders the State to secure a living wage, decent conditions of work and social and cultural opportunities to all workers?

questions.q:
Read the statements below.
Assertion (A): Article 23 of the Indian Constitution prohibits forced labour.
Reason (R): Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 years.

Match List I with List II:
I. Article 19(1)(c)   ->   A. Right to work and education within economic capacity

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about labour provisions in the Indian Constitution:
I. Article 23 prohibits forced labour.
II. Article 19(1)(c) prohibits employment of children below 14 years.

questions.explanation: Article 24, not Article 19(1)(c), prohibits employment of children below 14 years, so statement II is incorrect.

quizzes.title: ILO: short answer set
quizzes.passage: Some international bodies are created to set common standards rather than to govern countries directly. The body discussed here is one of them, and its concern is the working life of people across the world. It was set up under the Treaty of Versailles and was later linked with the United Nations. Its central aim is to improve labour conditions and living standards throughout the world. Its structure gives an equal voice to three groups: governments, employers and workers. This allows disagreements about working conditions to be discussed through a common process. The organisation has four stated objectives. It seeks to promote fundamental labour rights, create greater opportunities for women and men, enhance social protection and strengthen social dialogue. Its legal instruments take two forms. Conventions and Protocols are legally binding treaties, while Recommendations are non-binding guidelines. Some of its standards form part of the wider United Nations human rights framework. The organisation also publishes reports on employment, wages, social protection and youth. Its Director General leads the organisation's work. The work covers workers in many countries, including India, which is one of its founding members. Taken together, these standards and reports show how an international body can influence labour conditions.
